6.1 — Gravity & Jump: The First Flick

The cave is the first place in this game where down means something. Your character has spent five units as a top-down walker with gravity switched off — and it shows. Walk off the edge of the cave floor and you do not fall: you keep walking, level, for as long as you hold the key. Today you turn gravity back on for one scene, and then you use the same body to throw the character into the air.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I jump?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

The character falls, and then it jumps. "Make the player jump" is the whole feature, and it is really two mechanisms wearing one name: a world that pulls you down, and one instant where the body is handed an upward velocity that the pulling-down then spends. Neither half exists in the cave today, and the same prefab has to keep NOT falling in the top-down world you built it for.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the Player a body that falls in this sceneBody Type Dynamic and Gravity Scale above zero - it takes both. Dynamic is the setting from 2.1 that lets the world stop you; Gravity Scale is a multiplier on the project-wide gravity (Project Settings, Physics 2D, -9.81 on Y) and decides how hard the pull is. Your body has been Dynamic with Gravity Scale 0 since 2.1, so only the second half changes.Read: the rb.gravityScale row of the quick reference and the Body Type warning under that table - and the Dynamic + Gravity Scale 0 recipe you followed in 2.1.
  2. Tell the script which world it woke up inThe same prefab is played in both worlds, so "am I in the cave?" cannot live on the prefab - it is a fact about the *scene*. One serialized bool, ticked on the Player copy standing in the cave and left alone on the copy standing in the Overworld, is the entire mechanism. It is the hasAxe shape from 5.1 - a yes/no in the class body - pointed at the world instead of at the player.Read: the [SerializeField] private bool row in the quick reference, the field you declared in 5.1, and the [SerializeField] slot pattern from 1.3.
  3. Turn gravity on once, when the scene loadsA gated write in Start(): if the flag is on, hand the body a gravity scale. Once, before the first frame - the same "capture it before anything reads it" rule that seeded the turret's cooldown in 3.3. Put it in Update() instead and the same number is written sixty times a second, which looks identical and is still the wrong place for a fact that changes once per scene.Read: the void Start() row of the quick reference - runs once, first frame - and the cooldown field 3.3 seeded in Start().
  4. Notice one press of the jump keyInput.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) inside the Update() you have been adding to since 1.4. GetKeyDown is true on the single frame the key goes down; GetKey is true on every frame it is held. A jump is a moment, not a state - the same pair you met on the mouse in 1.6 and on the E key in 5.2.Read: the Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) row of the quick reference - it names this lesson - and the key check you wrote for the lever in 5.2.
  5. Hand the body one upward flick, and let gravity spend itAddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse): one instant change in momentum, applied at the next physics step. The height comes from the impulse divided by mass, the rise is paid for frame by frame by the gravity you switched on in part 1, and the apex is the frame where the vertical velocity reaches zero. Nothing else in the file has to know any of that.Read: the rb.AddForce(... ForceMode2D.Impulse) and rb.gravityScale rows of the quick reference, and the rb.linearVelocity = v row from 2.2 for what the force is turned into.

Three of those five parts are work you have already done: a Dynamic body is 2.1, a serialized slot in the class body is 1.3 and again 5.1, and a once-only write in Start() is 3.3. The other two have no precedent anywhere in this course, and they are why this lesson is a full walkthrough rather than a guided one. Part 2 is the first time you decide something about the *world* instead of about the player - every flag you have ever written (hasAxe, coins, lastAttackTime) was a fact about your character, and this one is a fact about where the character is standing. Part 5 is the first time you hand the physics engine a *force* rather than a velocity: everything you have moved since 1.4 was a speed you chose, and a flick is a shove you do not control the consequences of.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the player jump" cannot be looked up - there is no such API. "Push a rigidbody upward once" can: that is AddForce with a force mode, and it is one search away.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

The flag in part 2 is the first thing you have ever stored about the world rather than about the player. Name one other thing in your game that is really a fact about the scene, and say where you would keep it.

Part 4 notices a key press; part 5 moves the body. Nothing in the file measures time, and yet the arc has a height. Say where the height actually comes from - and which of the two parts you would change first if the jump felt wrong.

In 2.1 you set Body Type to Dynamic and Gravity Scale to 0, and in 2.2 you argued with the documentation about why the body had to stay Dynamic. Which part of today is that same pair of settings - and which one of the two changes?

In 5.1 the axe was a bool in the class body, ticked in the Inspector, and the whole design turned on what it started at. Which part of today is that same field, and what is it a fact about this time?

In 1.6 you chose between GetMouseButton and GetMouseButtonDown, and in 5.2 you chose between GetKey and GetKeyDown, both times because the wrong one fires every frame. Which part of today is that same choice, and what does the wrong one do to a jump?

The Problem: The Cave Has No Down ~15 min

Your goal: fall, then jump. Open Assets/_Scenes/Platformer.unity — the cave — and press Play. Walk left and right: that still works, because the movement you built in 1.4 and rewired in 2.2 does not care what the world looks like. Now walk off the edge of the floor and watch.

Nothing happens. You do not fall, and you do not jump. And neither of those is a bug in your code — they are both consequences of a decision you made two units ago. The Rigidbody2D you gave the Player in 2.1 has Gravity Scale 0, because a top-down character who obeys gravity falls through the world forever. You were right then. The cave is the first place in the game where you are wrong.

Discover it before you write anything:

  • Select the Player while the game is running. Find Gravity Scale on the Rigidbody2D, set it to 1, and watch what the character does. Then set it to 0.2. Describe the difference out loud.
  • Stop Play mode. Look at Gravity Scale again. What happened to the number you just typed? Inspector edits during Play are thrown away on Stop — which is exactly why the next step has to be code, not a checkbox.
  • Now select the Player in the Overworld scene — the top-down hub — and set Gravity Scale to 1 there, then press Play. This is the trap in the other direction. Write down what it costs.
  • Open the cave scene, select the Player standing in it, and look at PlayerController in the Inspector. The project has left you the answer. Read on — this one needs a paragraph of its own.
Somebody already decided how this script learns which scene it is in. The cave scene's copy of the Player has been carrying an override called isPlatformer since before this course existed. It is a leftover from the version of PlayerController.cs that shipped with the project, and it is invisible today because the stub you were given has no field by that name. But it is evidence, and it is worth knowing how to read: the project's own answer to "which world am I in?" was a serialized bool, ticked on the scene copy. Unity keys those overrides by field name, so declaring a field with exactly that name normally brings the tick back with it. You will do that below — and you will check the box rather than trust it.
Two physics facts, and they are independent. A body only falls if it is Dynamic and its Gravity Scale is above zero — either one alone does nothing, and each of them is a setting you already own. And a jump is not "move up": it is a change in velocity that physics then spends over the next half second. Gravity and jumping are the same mechanic seen from two sides.
Field on the Rigidbody2DWhat it actually does
Body Type Dynamic bodies fall and are pushed. Kinematic bodies only move where code puts them and ignore gravity, forces and mass entirely. Static never moves. If your character stands still in mid-air with Gravity Scale 5, look here first — a Static or Kinematic body is the only thing that can ignore a gravity scale that is plainly set.
Gravity Scale A multiplier on the project-wide gravity (Project Settings, Physics 2D, Y at -9.81). 0 is off; 1 is Earth; about 0.17 is the moon; 3 is a dropped anvil. It only means anything on a Dynamic body.
Mass How much the same force moves you. Gravity pulls harder on a heavy body, so mass partly cancels itself out and the fall barely changes — but a force you apply by hand divides by mass. Raise mass and your jump gets lower while your fall stays roughly the same.
Linear Damping Drag. Bleeds off speed over time, in the air as well as on the ground. Useful for a floaty "air resistance" feel; a value of 0 keeps your arc a clean parabola.
Constraints Freeze Rotation Z is the one you set in 2.2 so your character stops tumbling. It still matters in the air: an unfrozen body spins when it clips a corner mid-jump, and the sprite spins with it.

Socratic: Gravity Is a Number You Own

  1. Real gravity is a constant of the universe. Unity ships it as an Inspector field. Why would a game engine make a law of physics editable per object?
  2. Your top-down scene needs Gravity Scale 0 and your cave needs it above 0. Same Player prefab, same script, two different worlds. Where should that difference live — in the script, in the scene, or in both?
  3. A Kinematic body ignores gravity, forces and mass entirely. If you set Body Type to Kinematic in the cave, what would your jump code have to do instead to look like a jump?
  4. Mass barely changes how fast you fall but strongly changes how high you jump. Explain why one number treats the two cases differently.
  5. You can hold a body in the air forever by leaving Gravity Scale at 0 in the cave. Name a game genre where that is a feature rather than a bug.
Read Function-Level Examples ~10 min

None of these is from a video game, and none of them is more than a line. Read each one for what it does in isolation, then decide how it maps onto a jump — the last three are the ones worth arguing with, because they are about when a number matters rather than what it is.

Example 1 — The difference between a hand and a flick (bowling alley):

// A steady push applied every physics step is a hand on the ball.
// An impulse is one flick. Same total push. Completely different sport.

Example 2 — A forklift lifting a pallet:

liftBody.AddForce(Vector2.up * forkStrength, ForceMode2D.Impulse); // one shove

Example 3 — A submarine blowing its ballast tanks:

hull.linearVelocity = new Vector2(hull.linearVelocity.x, riseRate); // keep drift, set rise

Example 4 — A weather balloon (comment only):

// A balloon is not "anti-gravity". It is a body with a tiny gravity scale
// and a huge drag, so it rises slowly and stops rising.

Example 5 — A trampoline inspection rig (comment only):

// The height of a bounce is a velocity the moment the feet leave the mat.
// Everything after that is gravity spending it.

Predict Before Building

  1. In the forklift example, what would change if you removed the ForceMode2D.Impulse argument? Predict the behaviour in one sentence, then test both in your cave.
  2. The submarine keeps its horizontal drift and overwrites only the vertical part. What does that tell you about which component of a velocity a jump should touch — and which component it must leave alone?
  3. The balloon rises with a tiny gravity scale, and your top-down world used gravity scale 0. What is the difference between nothing falls and something rises?
  4. On the trampoline, height is decided at the instant the feet leave the mat. After that, does the player's input matter at all in a plain jump?
  5. The bowling example says the same total push can be two different shots. Which of the two would you pick for a jump, and what would the other one be used for in your game?
Read the Docs: How Does a Jump Get Into the Air? ~20 min

There is no Jump() in Unity, and nobody is going to give you one. There are four defensible ways to get a Dynamic body off the ground. Read all four before you pick — the walkthrough below builds the first row, and you are going to live with your choice for the rest of the year.

TechniqueHow it worksWhat it requiresWhat it feels likeThe cost
AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse) One instant change in momentum. You never touch velocity yourself; physics spends it over the following frames. A Dynamic body and Gravity Scale above 0. The classic flick. Arc is a clean parabola. Mass divides into it, so retuning mass silently retunes every jump in the game.
linearVelocity = new Vector2(x, jumpSpeed) You overwrite the vertical half of the velocity directly. Physics still owns everything after that. A Dynamic body and Gravity Scale above 0. Identical height every single time, to the pixel. It erases whatever vertical motion was already there — a moving platform's lift, a knockback, a bounce.
AddForce(Vector2.up * thrust, ForceMode2D.Force) every frame while held A continuous push, applied each physics step the key is down. This is what you get by accident if you forget the force mode. A Dynamic body; some rule that stops it (fuel, ceiling, timer). A rocket, not a jump. Height depends on how long you hold. It is flight. Without a limit your player leaves the level and never comes back.
MovePosition() in steps Code hands the body a target position and it moves there in steps. It never has a velocity you set — and a Kinematic body arrives at the target whatever it passes through on the way. A Kinematic body, moved in FixedUpdate. Perfectly controlled, weightless, and no arc. A Kinematic body ignores gravity, so it never falls — and it only collides with Dynamic bodies, so no wall, floor or platform is solid to it and no OnCollision* message fires against those static colliders. The cave door that switches scenes runs on OnCollisionEnter2D and would go silent. You would be writing gravity, walls and collision messages yourself — the things you came here to stop doing.
ForceMode2D.Force versus ForceMode2D.Impulse in one sentence. Force is a push that keeps applying while you keep calling it; Impulse is a single hit. Forget the argument and you get Force — which is a dribble, not a jump. That is the single most common "my jump does nothing" bug in this unit.

Choose, Then Justify

  1. Which of the four did you choose, and what does it require you to set on the Rigidbody2D that the other three do not?
  2. Row two gives the same height every time; row one gives a height that depends on mass. Which is easier to explain to a teammate in six months, and which is easier to retune?
  3. Row three is the only one where holding the key keeps mattering. Is that a jump or a jetpack — and what would have to be true about your level design for a jetpack to be fair?
  4. Row four puts the body in Kinematic. Read the table in 2.2 again: what did a Kinematic body cost you there — and is the price the same here, or do you pay it twice?
  5. Whatever you choose, the jump is one line. So what is the actual engineering work of this lesson?
  6. Would an enemy or a projectile want the same row as the player? Argue a position before you answer.
Build It With MeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how does my script know it is in the cave?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. The cave and the Overworld play the same prefab, so "which world am I in" cannot live on the prefab: it is a fact about the scene, and it has to reach the script before the first frame runs. Four lines, one ticked box, and two Play runs - the second one matters as much as the first. This is also the first flag in this course that is about the world instead of about your character.

Step 1Declare the flag, and get its starting value right

One field, in the class body, beside moveSpeed and your other serialized slots. It is the [SerializeField] private pattern from 1.3, and the exact shape of hasAxe from 5.1.

    [SerializeField] private bool isPlatformer = false;
  1. 1Which world this Player woke up in. false is the default, so a Player dropped into any scene that nobody has told otherwise keeps the top-down behaviour it has had since 2.1.The name is not free, and you can check why. Open the cave scene, click the Player, and look at PlayerController: the scene has been carrying an override called isPlatformer since before this course existed. It is a leftover from the version of this script that shipped with the project, and it is the project telling you which of the four options below it chose. Unity stores those overrides by field name, so declaring a field with exactly that name normally brings the tick back with it the moment the script recompiles - and naming it inCave loses it, because nothing matches. Check the box either way; tick it yourself if it is not already on.

Step 2Hand the body a gravity scale, once, and only in this world

The body lookup you have had in Start() since 2.2 is unchanged. What is new is one line underneath it, wrapped in the flag.

        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();

        if (isPlatformer)
        {
            body.gravityScale = 1f;
        }
  1. 1The reference you already cache here - the body you are about to give a gravity scale to. It is on the same GameObject as this script, which is why GetComponent is the right search, and it happens once, never inside Update().
  2. 3The gate. Read it as "if this Player is standing in the cave". It is the only thing separating the two worlds, and it is what keeps the next line from running in the Overworld.One flag, read once, in a method that runs once. Start() is the once-only setup method from 1.3 - the same one that finds your body and seeds your memory in every other script you own. A fact about the scene is exactly the kind of thing it is for.
  3. 4Opens the "this is the cave" block.
  4. 5The whole of turning gravity on. body.gravityScale is the Rigidbody2D property behind the Inspector field you have been reading all year, and 1f means "the project gravity, undiluted" - Project Settings, Physics 2D has Y at -9.81, and this number multiplies it.Why this has to be code and not just a number in the Inspector. You could set the cave copy to 1 and the Overworld copy to 0 by hand and write nothing at all - and the project itself left evidence that it did exactly that for the Overworld copy. But a number typed into the Inspector is invisible to a reader of your script, it has to be repeated on every new Player you place, and it cannot be reasoned about: nobody looking at Update() can tell which way is down. Writing it here makes the decision reviewable. The Bug Hunt asks you to try the Inspector-only version and say what it costs.
  5. 6Closes the gate. Past this line the two worlds are indistinguishable again - and that is the point: everything else in this file is shared.

Step 3Tick the box - in the cave scene, not on the prefab

This step is not code, and it is the one people get wrong. The flag has to be true on the Player standing in the cave and false everywhere else.

// Platformer scene ▸ Player ▸ PlayerController ▸ Is Platformer  =  ON
// Overworld scene ▸ Player ▸ PlayerController ▸ Is Platformer  =  OFF
  1. 1Open the cave scene, select the Player standing in it, and find the slot you declared in step 1. Tick it.Edit the instance, not the prefab. The prefab is a starting point that every scene copies; the cave scene holds one *instance* of it, and a change made there is an override that belongs to that scene alone. Tick the prefab instead and every scene falls - including the top-down Overworld. That is the same prefab-versus-instance rule 2.4 made you break on purpose and 5.1 made you repair, used here for the first time to store a fact about a scene rather than about an object.
  2. 2Then open the Overworld and check the other copy is unticked. It should be, because false is the default - but go and look, because the whole design rests on it.

Step 4Press Play twice - and treat the second run as the test

The cave is the obvious run. The Overworld is the one that tells you whether you gated anything.

// Cave: press Play. The character should drop to the floor immediately.
// Overworld: press Play. It must be exactly what it was before.
  1. 1It should fall the instant the scene loads, without you touching a key - that is gravity, and it is the first time in this project that the character has moved for a reason you did not press.The fall is not a bug to tune away. A platformer character that stands exactly where you placed it and waits is the character you have had for five units; the whole of Unit 6 depends on this one behaviour being real before you build anything on top of it.
  2. 2No fall, walking as before, coins still collected. If the Overworld changed, your gate is not working - and the most likely reason is that the tick went on the prefab instead of on the cave copy.This is the real test, and it is the one the Checkpoint asks about. "Does the cave work" is a question about one scene; "does the other scene still work" is a question about your design. A change made for the cave that quietly alters the top-down hub is the exact failure this flag exists to prevent.

Where this goes wrong

These are the mistakes this step actually produces. Read them before you are surprised by one.

  • the flag left unticked on the cave copy of the Player

    You will seeNothing at all happens. The character stands in mid-air wherever you placed it, the Console is clean, and the jump you are about to write appears to do nothing.

    Do thisTick it, on the scene instance. A serialized bool defaults to false, so an unticked box is the same thing as a gate that never opens - and because it fails silently, this is the first thing to check before you suspect your code.

  • the tick put on the Player PREFAB instead of on the cave copy

    You will seeThe cave works - and so does the Overworld, which now falls. Your top-down character slides off the bottom of the screen the moment you press Play there, and the coin you were walking toward is unreachable.

    Do thisUntick the prefab and tick the instance in the cave. A prefab is copied by every scene that uses it; only a value stored on the instance is a fact about that scene. Same rule as the axe collider in 5.1 and the enemy collider in 4.1.

  • body.gravityScale = 1f; written without the if, or moved into Update()

    You will seeBoth scenes fall. The Overworld has no floor, so the character is gone within a second - and because the line runs sixty times a second, nothing in the Console points at it.

    Do thisKeep the gate, and keep the whole thing in Start(). Gravity is decided once per scene; a line in Update() re-decides it every frame, which happens to look identical and is still the wrong home for a value that never changes.

  • the Rigidbody2D added to the Sprite child in Unit 2, so GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>() finds nothing

    You will seeNullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object, in Start(), on the line that writes gravityScale - before the first frame, before you have pressed anything.

    Do thisGetComponent<T>() looks only on the object the script is attached to. If your body ended up on the child, either move it up to the Player root or look it up with GetComponentInChildren<Rigidbody2D>() - the same call you already use for the Animator. Check the Inspector rather than assuming: this is the wiring fault that produces a code-shaped error.

Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. The walkthrough wrote the gravity scale as an if that only touches the cave; this version decides the number for both worlds in one ternary, which is the same behaviour and a different argument - "the Overworld keeps 0 because I said so" rather than "the Overworld keeps 0 because I never mentioned it". Both are right; pick the one you can defend. Your flag name, your gravity number and the place you put the line are yours. What has to match is the shape: a fact about the scene, read once in Start(), gating a write to the body.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

// PlayerController.cs - the gravity half, complete. Everything from 1.4 to 5.3
// (input, movement, animation, coins, health) stays exactly as you wrote it;
// the flag and the one line under it are the whole of what is new.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;      // your number from 2.2
    [SerializeField] private bool isPlatformer = false; // which world did I wake up in?

    private Rigidbody2D body;

    void Start()
    {
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();             // looked up once, per 2.2

        // Decided once, for both worlds. The Overworld's 0 is written here
        // rather than inherited from the prefab, so the decision is visible
        // to anyone reading this file instead of only to the Inspector.
        body.gravityScale = isPlatformer ? 1f : 0f;
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // ... the input, movement and animation lines from 1.4, 1.6, 2.2 and 5.3 ...
    }
}
Build It With MeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I make the character leave the ground?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. There is no Jump() in Unity, and nobody is going to give you one. The gravity half is already in your file, so what is left is four lines: a number to tune, a key check, one push, and a way to see that it worked. The push is where every mistake in this lesson happens.

Step 1Declare how hard the flick is

One field, in the class body, next to moveSpeed. Same [SerializeField] private pattern, and the same reason: it is a number a designer tunes, not a number you type into a condition.

    [SerializeField] private float jumpForce = 7f;
  1. 1How hard the flick is. Named jumpForce because that is what it becomes - a force - so a reader never mistakes it for the speed the character leaves the ground at.This is a starting guess, not a value. The number that makes a jump feel right is found by the tuning triangle at the bottom of this page, one change at a time, never by reasoning about it in advance. And notice what it is not: a force divided by mass gives a velocity, so the height you get from 7f depends on the body mass the Inspector is showing. That coupling is the price of using a force, and it is the first row of the technique table above.

Step 2Notice the press, once, at the bottom of Update()

Four lines at the end of the Update() you have been adding to since 1.4, after your movement and animation lines, beside the key check you already wrote for the lever.

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            body.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
        }
  1. 1The new key question. Input is the class from 1.4, KeyCode.Space names the key, and GetKeyDown is true on the single frame the key goes down.Input.GetKey(KeyCode.Space) is the wrong one, and it fails in the loudest way there is. Without the Down it is true on every frame the key is held, so half a second of holding Space applies sixty pushes, one per frame, and the character leaves the top of the level. The jump looks broken; it is not, the condition is. This is the same pair you met on the mouse in 1.6 and on the E key in 5.2 - and the third time you have been asked to tell a moment from a state.
  2. 2Opens the "Space went down this frame" block.
  3. 3The flick. Vector2.up is (0, 1) - straight up - scaled by the field from step 1. AddForce is the physics engine's own way of changing momentum, so you never touch the velocity yourself.The second argument is the whole lesson, and leaving it out is the classic bug. With ForceMode2D.Impulse this is one hit, applied once, at the next physics step. Without it the default is ForceMode2D.Force - a push that keeps applying while the calls keep coming - and because this line is inside a check that is true on exactly one frame, you get a dribble so small the character twitches and settles. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and "my jump does nothing" is what you write in the group chat. Read the call as a sentence: add a force, upward, of this size, as an impulse.
  4. 4Closes the key-press block. Update() carries on and ends exactly as it did before.

Step 3Prove the arc in the Console, then take the proof out

There is no UI for vertical velocity, so the Console is your instrument. Two lines, and the second one is the interesting one.

            Debug.Log("Flick. v.y = " + body.linearVelocity.y);
        Debug.Log("v.y = " + body.linearVelocity.y);
// Delete both prints before you move on
  1. 1A temporary print inside the block, after the push. body.linearVelocity is the movement method you chose in 2.2, read instead of written, and its .y is the half a jump cares about.**Read it once and notice it prints the speed from *before* the flick.** AddForce does not change linearVelocity at the instant you call it - the force is applied when the physics engine next runs - so this line reports the velocity the body had going into the jump. That is not a bug; it is the clearest possible proof that a force and a velocity are two different things.
  2. 2A second, temporary print at the bottom of Update(), outside the key block, with no condition on it. Watch the number while you play.That number is the parabola. It jumps to a positive peak the moment you press Space, shrinks every frame as gravity takes it back, crosses zero at the top of the arc, and grows negative all the way down. Up, zero, down - and you have just watched the entire mathematics of a jump without writing a line of it. The apex is not a place in your code; it is the frame where this number passes through nothing.
  3. 3They were an instrument, not a feature. The proof is that you saw the number turn around.Update() runs sixty times a second, so an un-deleted print here is a Console filling with a thousand lines a minute for the rest of the unit - and it will bury the next real error under it. Same rule as the hasAxe print in 5.1.

Step 4Know where these lines belong, and where they must not go

Two clocks run in a Unity project and the jump touches both. This step is a rule, not code - and it is the last thing to check when a jump feels unreliable rather than wrong.

// Input and the key check:  Update()
// The push:  fine from Update(), applied at the next physics step
  1. 1Every frame, once per rendered frame. Input.GetKeyDown is true for exactly one of those frames, so one press is one true.A key check in FixedUpdate() can fire twice or not at all. FixedUpdate is the physics clock and it does not run once per frame: on a slow machine it can run several times inside one frame, and on a fast one it can skip frames entirely. A press that lasts one frame can therefore be counted twice or missed completely, and the bug shows up on somebody else's computer rather than yours.
  2. 2AddForce called from Update() is not a mistake. The force is queued, and the physics engine applies it on its own clock - which is exactly why one frame of key press produces one clean impulse.This is the part people get backwards. The instinct is that anything touching the body belongs in FixedUpdate, and for a velocity you are setting every frame that is right - it is why your movement from 2.2 can live in Update() too and still behave. Forces are the exception: the engine collects them and spends them on its own schedule. Keep the input where input belongs, and let the engine own the timing.

Where this goes wrong

These are the mistakes this step actually produces. Read them before you are surprised by one.

  • ForceMode2D.Impulse left off the AddForce call

    You will seeThe character twitches a hair and settles back down. It looks like the jump is too weak, so you raise jumpForce, and it still looks like the jump is too weak.

    Do thisAdd the argument. Without it you get ForceMode2D.Force, which is a push that keeps applying only while you keep calling it - and you call it on one frame out of sixty. Impulse is one hit. This is the single most common "my jump does nothing" bug in this unit.

  • Input.GetKey(KeyCode.Space) - the version without Down

    You will seeHold Space and the character climbs. Not a jump: a continuous ascent with no ceiling, because sixty presses a second are being applied one after another.

    Do thisGetKeyDown is true on the one frame the key goes down; GetKey is true on every frame it is held. A jump is a moment, not a state - the same pair as GetMouseButton and GetMouseButtonDown in 1.6, and the same trap.

  • the key check moved into FixedUpdate()

    You will seeIt works - most of the time. Then on someone else's machine in the lab, one press in ten does nothing at all, and occasionally one press does two jumps in the air.

    Do thisPoll input in Update(). FixedUpdate is the physics clock and does not run once per frame, so a condition that is true for exactly one frame can be seen twice or missed. GetKeyDown and FixedUpdate are the one combination in this lesson that is wrong on somebody else's hardware and right on yours.

  • the flick written in a scene where the flag was never ticked

    You will seePress Space and the character rises - and keeps rising. There is no apex, no fall, and no error: the game simply has no ceiling, and the top-down Overworld does the same thing.

    Do thisCheck gravityScale before you touch the jump code. An impulse with no gravity is not a weak jump, it is an escape: the number you were watching in the Console climbs forever instead of turning around. This is the trap callout at the bottom of the Build Lab, and it is worth producing on purpose once.

  • jumpForce tuned before the gravity number was settled

    You will seeYou spend twenty minutes doubling and halving the force, and every value feels wrong in a different way - floaty at 5, twitchy at 14, and never quite right in between.

    Do thisTune them as a pair, and change one at a time. Gravity decides how long the arc lasts and the force decides how high it goes, so a change to either one moves the apex. The tuning triangle below is the order: gravity first, then the force, then mass - and write one sentence of feel for each, or you will not remember which change did what.

Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Two differences are worth naming, and neither is a mistake. First the shape: the walkthrough wrote the push inline inside the key check, and this file gives it a method called Jump() - the same line, with a name you can point at when 6.2 and 6.3 start asking what a jump is allowed to do. Second the gravity line: this file decides the number for both worlds with a ternary where the walkthrough only wrote it for one. What has to match is the shape of the jump: a single-frame key check, one AddForce with ForceMode2D.Impulse, and a world that is already pulling down before you press anything. Your key, your number, and the names of your own methods are yours.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

// PlayerController.cs - gravity for the cave, and one flick upward.
// The gravity half came first; the jump assumes it. Up, apex, down: the
// only line that makes the arc is the force, and gravity does the rest.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;      // your number from 2.2
    [SerializeField] private float jumpForce = 7f;      // how hard the flick is
    [SerializeField] private bool isPlatformer = false; // which world did I wake up in?

    private Rigidbody2D body;

    void Start()
    {
        // Looked up once, never inside Update() - the rule from 2.2.
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();

        // Decided once, for both worlds.
        body.gravityScale = isPlatformer ? 1f : 0f;
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // ... input, movement and animation, from 1.4 to 5.3 ...

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            Jump();
        }
    }

    // The whole jump. One impulse, and gravity spends it over the next half
    // second - which is why there is nothing here about coming back down.
    private void Jump()
    {
        body.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
    }
}
Build Lab: Turn Gravity On, Then Jump ~30 min

Step 0 — inventory. Select the Player in the cave scene and list what is on it: Transform, PlayerController, whatever you added in Unit 2 — and the child Sprite carrying the SpriteRenderer and Animator. Confirm a Rigidbody2D and a Collider2D are both there. If you added them to a scene instance instead of the prefab in Unit 2, the prefab may still be bare — fix that first, or every scene you build from here inherits the problem.

Architectural specification: how does your script know it is in the cave? Your movement code currently assumes a top-down world. The cave needs the opposite assumptions, and the script has to be told which world it woke up in. The walkthrough built the third option below, because that is the one the project itself left evidence of. Options, all of them used in real projects:
  • (a) Ask the scene its name — SceneManager.GetActiveScene().name compared against "Platformer" in Start(). Readable, and it breaks silently if someone renames the scene.
  • (b) Ask the scene its build index — the cave is index 2. Numbers do not break when a scene is renamed, but they lie when the build order changes. SceneSwitch.cs already uses this for scene switching, so read it before you borrow the idea.
  • (c) A serialized bool on the prefab, ticked per scene instance — you can see it in the Inspector without pressing Play, and this is what the cave scene's leftover isPlatformer override says the project chose. The cost is that every new scene needs someone to remember to tick it.
  • (d) A separate component that only exists on the cave's Player — the component's presence is the flag. Costs one more file and a GetComponent.
  • Whatever you pick: if you already built a scene-mode flag earlier in the year, reuse it. Two flags that both mean "which world am I in" is how a project starts rotting.
Architectural specification: gravity.
  • Where does the cave's gravity get turned on? Name the exact point in the lifecycle — a field default, Start(), or every frame — and say what breaks at each of the other two.
  • If you write gravityScale = 1 inside Update() unconditionally, what happens to the top-down Overworld? Go and check rather than guessing.
  • You could skip the code entirely: select the cave copy, type 1 into Gravity Scale, and select the Overworld copy and type 0. It works. Do it once, then write one sentence on what a reader of your script now cannot see.
  • What value do you start with for the cave — 1, 3, 0.5? Write down the number and one word for the feel, before you tune it.
  • Your movement line from 2.2 reads Vertical as well as Horizontal, so pressing W in the cave still lifts the character straight up. Your flag is already the gate for that. You do not have to fix it today — but write down where the fix would go.
  • Is your top-down scene still correct after this change? The test is not "does the cave work" — it is "does the other scene still work".
Architectural specification: the flick.
  • Which key, and which of GetKey or GetKeyDown? What does holding the key for two seconds do under each one?
  • Where does the Rigidbody2D reference come from, and when do you cache it? Does it live on the same GameObject as your script, or on the child Sprite? Look before you type.
  • Does the jump belong in Update() or FixedUpdate()? The key check and the force have different answers — say which is which and why.
  • What is the magnitude — a serialized field so a designer can tune it, or a magic number? And does it name a force or a speed? The name you give it decides what the next person thinks it does.
  • How do you know it worked? Write the Console line that proves the jump fired, and the second one that proves gravity is pulling you back down.

The tuning triangle. Change one number at a time and write one sentence of feel for each, in a file you keep:

KnobTryThe sentence you write
jump forcehalf, then double"how high" — arcade versus ant
Gravity Scale0.2 → 1 → 4"how heavy" — moon versus dropped stone
Mass1 → 5how much the same push moves you — and whether your fall changed at all
Gravity off plus an impulse is not a jump — it is an escape. If the cave's Player keeps Gravity Scale 0 and you add an impulse, the character rises and never stops rising. There is no error and no warning; the game simply has no ceiling. When a jump "works but feels wrong", check Gravity Scale and Body Type before you touch your code.
Bug Hunt: The Physics Faults ~15 min

Bug Hunt

  1. Remove the ForceMode2D.Impulse argument and keep the force. Tap the key. What did the jump become, and why does a "dribble" look like nothing at all in a single frame?
  2. Set Body Type to Kinematic and press the key. With the technique you chose, does anything move at all? Which line of the Body Type documentation explains your answer?
  3. Set Gravity Scale to 0 in the cave with the jump code still in place. Describe the first two seconds after one press — and why is "no gravity" worse than "no jump"?
  4. Jump in the cave and watch the camera. Does it follow you upward? Find the component on Main Camera, read its fields, and work out which setting is holding it still. (Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts is worth knowing by now.)
  5. Set Gravity Scale to 8 and jump onto a raised platform. Where do you land relative to where you aimed, and what does that tell you about tuning gravity and jump force as a pair?
  6. Leave the jump in Update(), then move the key check into FixedUpdate() and hold the key down through a slow frame. Do you see any difference at 60 fps? When would you see it — and on whose laptop?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Jump Design

  1. Tune a "sticky" jump and a "floaty" one — two very different pairs of gravity and force. Which one suits a cave full of hazards, and what does each do to how far ahead a player can see?
  2. Variable jump height, the classic: releasing the key early produces a shorter hop. Which single quantity would you cut off mid-rise, and why is that fairer than it sounds?
  3. Make the character jump downward through a platform. What has to be true about the platform's collider for that to work at all?
  4. Untick the camera's vertical lock and play your cave again. What does the room read like now, and what does the camera do at the top of a jump?
  5. Try a jump from a moving platform. Which of your four techniques would survive the ride, and which would fight it?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain Gravity Scale, Body Type and Mass as three separate ideas, not one
  • Say where the cave's gravity gets turned on, and prove the top-down world still works
  • Compare the four ways to leave the ground and defend the one you wrote
  • Explain Force versus Impulse in feel-words
  • Explain the parabola: a velocity that gravity spends, an apex, and a fall
  • Explain GetKeyDown versus GetKey for one-shot actions
  • Commit and push
